source.title: On the Generalization Mystery in Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: The study measures per-example gradient coherence and reports training/generalization outcomes on real and randomized data; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment as its main intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on Gaussian-noise inputs, random-label datasets, and mixed noisy data. Results cited from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are excluded. Figure-only results are recorded without reconstructing plotted values.
record.test_reason: The study conducts its own SGD experiments on randomized labels and Gaussian inputs and measures training/test loss and accuracy, reproducing the original fitting question and measures. Its additional coherence analysis does not make those experiments a different-method test. Section 9 also directly tests learning order under label corruption.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' position. More precisely, they propose that aligned per-example gradients promote algorithmic stability and generalization, and provide theoretical and experimental evidence for this explanation. They show that correctly labeled examples are learned earlier than corrupted labels and that robust gradient aggregation can suppress memorization. Their generalization bound is explicitly qualitative and loose, and whole-network coherence sometimes requires a layer-wise analysis.
record.recipe_differences: Measures gradient coherence and compares ordinary SGD with robust gradient aggregation; the random-label experiments are supplementary rather than a reproduction centered on the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes the measured coherence pattern: ResNet-50 and AlexNet differ, with AlexNet showing surprisingly high whole-network coherence on random data. Layer-wise coherence can differ substantially from the whole-network measure. M3 outcomes depend on micro-batch size and learning rate; the authors report instability for some learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: M3 learns the real-image subset while failing to learn Gaussian replacement images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust gradient aggregation can suppress memorization of Gaussian inputs while retaining learning on real inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Ordinary SGD learns Gaussian replacement images later than real images in the mixed-input experiment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Real inputs are learned before unstructured Gaussian inputs during mixed-data training.

record.problems: The paper notes that whole-network coherence can obscure layer-level differences. Several additional random-label results are presented only in figures; exact outcome values are not stated in the text. Batch-normalization experiments use an imputed coherence measure.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Random-label training/test curves in Appendix E are figure-only; the text does not provide condition-specific numerical accuracy values beyond the stated training target.

untested.parts: Exact random-label training error and chance-level test performance cannot be established from the extracted curve text. Appendix E describes matched real/random experiments but selects the training configuration specifically to permit random-data fitting; it does not establish that an independently chosen original training recipe suffices.

No readable quantitative comparison establishes a small constant-factor training-time overhead or convergence slowdown across label-corruption fractions. Statements about slower learning under winsorization concern a modified optimizer.
Shuffled-pixel and independently permuted-pixel inputs are not tested.

The label-noise sweep is presented in Figure 4, but the supplied extraction does not preserve readable curves needed to assess perfect fitting and steady degradation toward chance. Figure 9 measures pristine/corrupt training dynamics, not the full test-error trajectory across corruption fractions.

Whether weight decay, dropout and data augmentation fail to prevent random-label fitting is not tested. Generalization without regularizers is demonstrated, but the effect of removing them is not isolated by a matched regularized comparison.

The direct label-corruption learning-order experiment uses ResNet-50 on ImageNet with 50% randomized labels; broader architectures, datasets and corruption fractions are not established by that experiment.

missing.what: The direct label-learning-order result: under 50% randomized ImageNet labels, pristine examples have higher coherence and are learned much faster than corrupt examples. Record the training-loss/accuracy trajectories separately; coherence alone is not the behavioral endpoint.

The separate A3/ordinary-SGD experiment with entirely Gaussian inputs reports memorization, whereas M3 fails to learn them. Record the ordinary-SGD fitting result with its distinct setup: learning rate 0.20, three micro-batches of 256, and 90 epochs.

record.verdict_notes: No files or external sources were consulted. The supplied figure text contains axes and legends but does not preserve the plotted curves reliably; no numerical endpoints or timing ratios were reconstructed. Consequently, no V1 or V4 verdict is assigned from unreadable curves or a training-selection target. Appendix E random-label curves and the MNIST label-noise sweep are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not duplicated in missing. The study is not either listed original source.

versions.untested_parts: The ResNet-50 experiment in Section 6 randomizes input pixels, not labels. Random-label results are discussed in Appendix E, but exact curves and values are figure-only.
No direct comparison of training time for true versus random labels or convergence slowdown by corruption fraction.
The study tests Gaussian-noise inputs; it does not report shuffled-pixel or independently permuted-pixel conditions.

The paper describes a 50% random-label ImageNet experiment and MNIST label-noise sweeps, but the separate training/test outcomes for those conditions are figure-only and not extracted as precise values.
The experiments omit explicit regularizers, but do not compare regularized and unregularized training to test whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation are necessary or sufficient.

The study tests a mixed dataset with half the ImageNet training images replaced by Gaussian noise, and separately reports a random-label experiment. It does not test learning order on completely random labels.
